cityEvents.title: Gaius Gracchus moves house to live among the poor
cityEvents.summary: To show his sympathy with the people, Gaius Gracchus left his house on the Palatine and moved to the district below the Forum where the poor and humble lived.
cityEvents.locName: the crowded district below the Forum
cityEvents.note: Plutarch's phrase 'the area below the agora' probably means the low quarters toward the Velabrum.

cityEvents.title: Gaius Gracchus pulls down the gladiators' stands
cityEvents.summary: Magistrates had built stands around the Forum to rent seats for a gladiatorial show; when they refused to remove them, Gracchus had his workmen tear them down in the night so the poor could watch free.
cityEvents.locName: temporary stands around the Forum square

cityEvents.title: The attendant Antyllus killed at the consul's sacrifice
cityEvents.summary: While the consul Opimius sacrificed on the Capitol, his attendant Antyllus insulted Gracchus' supporters and was stabbed to death with writing styluses. Opimius displayed the body in the Forum and obtained the senate's emergency decree.
cityEvents.locName: the Capitol, at the consul's morning sacrifice

cityEvents.title: Fulvius and Gracchus seize the Aventine
cityEvents.summary: Fulvius Flaccus armed his men with Gallic spoils from his house and occupied the Aventine around the Temple of Diana; Opimius attacked up the hill with infantry and Cretan archers and the Gracchans broke.
cityEvents.locName: the Temple of Diana on the Aventine

cityEvents.title: Two friends die holding the gate and bridge for Gaius
cityEvents.summary: As Gaius fled downhill, his friend Pomponius held his pursuers at the Porta Trigemina and Laetorius at the Pons Sublicius, both fighting until killed, so that Gaius could cross the river.
cityEvents.locName: the Porta Trigemina and the Pons Sublicius

cityEvents.title: Death of Gaius Gracchus in the grove of Furrina
cityEvents.summary: Gaius reached the sacred grove of Furrina on the Janiculum with one slave, Philocrates, who killed him and then himself. His head was cut off and brought to Opimius, who had promised its weight in gold; 3000 of his followers were later executed.
cityEvents.locName: the Lucus Furrinae on the Janiculum slope (site of the later Syrian sanctuary at Villa Sciarra)
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

cityEvents.title: 'Discord's work builds Concord's temple'
cityEvents.summary: Opimius restored the Temple of Concord at the foot of the Capitol to celebrate the restoration of order. One night someone carved beneath its inscription: 'A work of madness makes a temple of Concord'.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Concord below the Tabularium

cityEvents.title: Metellus rebuilds the Temple of Castor
cityEvents.summary: L. Caecilius Metellus Dalmaticus rebuilt the Temple of Castor on a high podium with a speakers' platform at its front, used thereafter for public meetings and legislative assemblies.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Castor

cityEvents.title: Three Vestals tried; another live burial in the Forum Boarium
cityEvents.summary: After the Vestal Helvia was killed by lightning, three Vestals were tried for unchastity with knights; two were condemned. The Sibylline books again required a Gallic and a Greek couple to be buried alive in the Forum Boarium, and the temple of Venus Verticordia was founded.
cityEvents.locName: Forum Boarium, and the Atrium Vestae

cityEvents.title: Jugurtha silenced before the people
cityEvents.summary: Brought to Rome under safe-conduct to testify, Jugurtha was presented to a contio in the Forum; when the tribune Memmius questioned him, the bribed tribune Baebius ordered him to keep silent. Leaving Rome, he is said to have called it 'a city for sale'.
cityEvents.locName: a contio before the Rostra

cityEvents.title: Jugurtha thrown into the Tullianum
cityEvents.summary: After walking in Marius' triumph Jugurtha was stripped, his earrings torn off with the lobes, and lowered into the underground cell of the Carcer. 'Hercules, how cold your bath is!' he said; he starved to death six days later.
cityEvents.locName: the Tullianum, lower chamber of the Carcer below the Capitol

cityEvents.title: Memmius beaten to death at the consular elections
cityEvents.summary: During the voting for the consuls of 99, Saturninus' and Glaucia's men clubbed to death the candidate C. Memmius in front of the assembly, turning opinion and the senate against them.
cityEvents.locName: the voting enclosure (Ovile/Saepta) of the Campus Martius
cityEvents.note: Appian places the murder 'in the midst of the voting'; consular elections were held in the Campus Martius.

cityEvents.title: The triumphal procession enters by the Porta Triumphalis
cityEvents.summary: Triumphs mustered in the Campus Martius near the Villa Publica and entered the city by the Porta Triumphalis by the Circus Flaminius, then passed through the Forum Boarium and the Circus Maximus, around the Palatine and down the Sacra Via to climb the Capitol.
cityEvents.locName: the Porta Triumphalis by the Circus Flaminius
cityEvents.note: Representative; the gate's position is disputed (near S. Omobono or the Circus Flaminius).

cityEvents.title: Saturninus stoned to death in the Curia
cityEvents.summary: Besieged on the Capitol after the senate's emergency decree, Saturninus, Glaucia and their followers surrendered to Marius, who shut them in the Curia Hostilia for safety. A mob climbed onto the roof, tore off the tiles and stoned them to death.
cityEvents.locName: inside the Curia Hostilia, struck through its roof

cityEvents.title: Livius Drusus stabbed in the atrium of his house
cityEvents.summary: Returning home from the Forum with a crowd of clients, the tribune M. Livius Drusus was stabbed with a cobbler's knife in the dark atrium of his house on the Palatine; he died saying the state would not soon find another like him. His death sparked the Social War.
cityEvents.locName: atrium of Drusus' house on the N slope of the Palatine (later Cicero's house)
cityEvents.note: Velleius tells how Drusus wanted the house open to every eye; it passed to Crassus and then Cicero. Site on the Palatine slope above the Forum, exact plot unknown.

cityEvents.title: Praetor Asellio murdered while sacrificing
cityEvents.summary: The praetor A. Sempronius Asellio, who had ruled in favour of debtors, was attacked by moneylenders while offering sacrifice before the Temple of Castor; he fled toward the Temple of Vesta and was killed in a nearby tavern.
cityEvents.locName: in front of the Temple of Castor

cityEvents.title: Riot at the Temple of Castor; Sulla hides in Marius' house
cityEvents.summary: Sulpicius' armed men broke up a meeting of the consuls by the Temple of Castor and killed the son of the consul Pompeius Rufus; Sulla escaped by taking refuge in the house of his enemy Marius before leaving for his army.
cityEvents.locName: the Forum by the Temple of Castor

cityEvents.title: Sulla fights his way in at the Esquiline
cityEvents.summary: Sulla's legions entered by the Esquiline Gate; met by a hail of tiles from the rooftops and Marius' improvised force at the Forum Esquilinum, Sulla seized a torch, ordered the houses burned and drove the Marians back toward the Temple of Tellus.
cityEvents.locName: the Forum Esquilinum inside the Porta Esquilina

cityEvents.title: Sulpicius' head displayed on the Rostra
cityEvents.summary: Betrayed by a slave, the tribune Sulpicius was killed and his head was set up on the Rostra, the first time a magistrate's head was displayed there.
cityEvents.locName: the Rostra

cityEvents.title: Consul Octavius killed in his chair on the Janiculum
cityEvents.summary: When Cinna and Marius took Rome, the consul Cn. Octavius refused to flee and sat in his robes on his curule chair on the Janiculum; Censorinus' horsemen cut off his head, the first consul's head to be hung on the Rostra.
cityEvents.locName: the Janiculum, where Octavius waited on his curule chair

cityEvents.title: The flamen Dialis Merula opens his veins at Jupiter's altar
cityEvents.summary: Summoned to trial by the Marians, L. Cornelius Merula, priest of Jupiter, took off his priestly cap, cut his veins in the Capitoline temple and spattered the god's altar with his blood, cursing his killers.
cityEvents.locName: inside the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus

cityEvents.title: Heads of senators on the Rostra: the Marian terror
cityEvents.summary: For five days Marius' slave bodyguard, the Bardyaei, killed whomever he did not greet; the heads of the orator M. Antonius and others were set on the Rostra.
cityEvents.locName: the Rostra

cityEvents.title: Marius Gratidianus' coinage edict and statues in every street
cityEvents.summary: The praetor Marius Gratidianus hurried from the tribunes' bench to the Rostra to publish alone the edict on the testing of debased coin; the grateful people set up his statues in every vicus with candles and incense.
cityEvents.locName: the Rostra; statues at the compita of every vicus

cityEvents.title: The Capitoline temple burns
cityEvents.summary: On 6 July 83 the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus burned to the ground, perhaps by accident, destroying the Sibylline books and the treasures of four centuries.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus

cityEvents.title: Gratidianus tortured to death at a family tomb
cityEvents.summary: In Sulla's proscriptions Catiline dragged Marius Gratidianus through the streets to the tomb of the Lutatii across the Tiber and there, at the grave of Catulus' father, broke his limbs and cut off his head.
cityEvents.locName: the tomb of the Lutatii across the Tiber
cityEvents.note: The tomb lay 'trans Tiberim'; site unknown.

cityEvents.title: Proscription lists posted in the Forum
cityEvents.summary: Sulla posted lists of the outlawed on whitened boards in the Forum; anyone could kill those named for a reward. The heads of the proscribed were piled at the Lacus Servilius at the head of the Vicus Iugarius.
cityEvents.locName: the Forum by the Rostra; heads at the Lacus Servilius

cityEvents.title: Heads of senators at the Lacus Servilius
cityEvents.summary: Seneca recalls the fountain basin at the head of the Vicus Iugarius as 'the spoliarium of Sulla's proscriptions', where the severed heads of senators were displayed.
cityEvents.locName: the Lacus Servilius at the Forum end of the Vicus Iugarius, by the W corner of the later Basilica Julia
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)

cityEvents.title: Battle of the Colline Gate
cityEvents.summary: Pontius Telesinus' Samnites, marching to destroy Rome, fought Sulla's army under the walls at the Colline Gate from late afternoon into the night. Sulla's left wing was driven against the gate, but Crassus won on the right and the Samnites were annihilated.
cityEvents.locName: outside the Porta Collina

cityEvents.title: Prisoners massacred in the Villa Publica
cityEvents.summary: Sulla addressed the senate in the Temple of Bellona while some 6000 Samnite prisoners penned in the nearby Villa Publica were butchered. As the senators started at the screams, Sulla told them to pay attention: some criminals were being punished on his orders.
cityEvents.locName: the Villa Publica, with Sulla speaking in the Temple of Bellona nearby

cityEvents.title: Sulla's triumph over Mithridates
cityEvents.summary: Sulla celebrated a two-day triumph with treasure from the East; returning exiles of the nobility followed his chariot calling him saviour and father.
cityEvents.locName: triumphal route along the Sacra Via

cityEvents.title: Sulla enlarges the senate house
cityEvents.summary: To seat his enlarged senate of 600, Sulla rebuilt and enlarged the Curia; the statues of Pythagoras and Alcibiades that had stood at the corners of the Comitium since the Samnite wars were removed.
cityEvents.locName: the Curia Hostilia / Cornelia and the corners of the Comitium

cityEvents.title: Sulla lays down the dictatorship in the Forum
cityEvents.summary: Sulla dismissed his lictors and bodyguard in the Forum and offered to account for his acts to anyone who asked; then he walked home through the crowd with his friends.
cityEvents.locName: the Forum

cityEvents.title: Sulla's funeral and cremation in the Campus Martius
cityEvents.summary: Sulla's body was carried in a golden litter from Puteoli; matrons' spices filled 210 litters and formed an effigy of him in frankincense. After the laudation from the Rostra, knights and senators bore him to the Campus Martius, where he was the first Cornelius to be cremated.
cityEvents.locName: pyre and tomb in the Campus Martius
cityEvents.note: The tomb was in the Campus Martius among the kings' burial places; exact site unknown.

cityEvents.title: Catulus builds the Tabularium
cityEvents.summary: Q. Lutatius Catulus built the great substructure and record office closing the Forum's west end beneath the Capitol, recording it in an inscription that still survives.
cityEvents.locName: the Tabularium on the E face of the Capitol

cityEvents.title: Lepidus' army beaten at the Milvian Bridge
cityEvents.summary: M. Aemilius Lepidus marched on the city at the head of disaffected Etruscans; Catulus and Pompey routed him at the Milvian Bridge and on the Janiculum outside the walls.
cityEvents.locName: the Milvian Bridge on the Via Flaminia

cityEvents.title: Pompey leads his horse before the censors
cityEvents.summary: During the review of the knights, the consul Pompey came down the Forum with his lictors leading his horse, and before the censors seated by the Temple of Castor declared that he had served all his campaigns under himself as general.
cityEvents.locName: censors' tribunal in the Forum near the Temple of Castor

cityEvents.title: The crowd's roar fells a crow over the Forum
cityEvents.summary: When the law giving Pompey command against the pirates was debated, the shout of the crowd in the Forum was so great that a crow flying over it fell stunned among them.
cityEvents.locName: above the Forum square

cityEvents.title: Caesar restores Marius' trophies on the Capitol by night
cityEvents.summary: As aedile, Caesar had gilded statues and Victories commemorating Marius' victories secretly made and set up on the Capitol overnight; at dawn veterans wept at the sight, while Catulus denounced him in the senate.
cityEvents.locName: the Capitol, at the site of Marius' trophies

cityEvents.title: Lightning strikes the Capitoline wolf
cityEvents.summary: Lightning struck statues on the Capitol, including the gilded she-wolf with the twins, the bronze tablets of the laws and an old statue of Jupiter; the haruspices foretold slaughter and civil strife, and a new statue of Jupiter was ordered facing east.
cityEvents.locName: statues on the Capitol

cityEvents.title: Caesar moves into the Domus Publica
cityEvents.summary: Elected pontifex maximus, Caesar left his modest house in the Subura for the official residence on the Sacra Via beside the Regia and the House of the Vestals.
cityEvents.locName: the Domus Publica on the Sacra Via

cityEvents.title: Birth of Octavian 'at the Oxheads'
cityEvents.summary: The future Augustus was born before sunrise on 23 September in a house on the Palatine at the place called Ad Capita Bubula, 'the Oxheads'; a shrine was later made there.
cityEvents.locName: Ad Capita Bubula on the Palatine (NE slope toward the Sacra Via)
cityEvents.note: Location of the Oxheads uncertain; usually placed on the NE side of the Palatine above the Sacra Via.

cityEvents.title: Cicero's First Catilinarian in the Temple of Jupiter Stator
cityEvents.summary: Cicero convened the senate in the fortified Temple of Jupiter Stator at the foot of the Palatine and attacked Catiline face to face: 'How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?' The senators left the benches around Catiline empty; he left Rome that night.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Jupiter Stator by the Porta Mugonia, at the top of the Sacra Via
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
cityEvents.note: The temple's site near the Arch of Titus is accepted but its remains are not securely identified.

cityEvents.title: Allobroges envoys arrested at the Milvian Bridge
cityEvents.summary: In the small hours of 3 December the praetors Flaccus and Pomptinus, posted at either end of the Milvian Bridge, ambushed the Allobrogian envoys and Volturcius leaving Rome with the conspirators' letters.
cityEvents.locName: both ends of the Milvian Bridge

cityEvents.title: Conspirators confronted in the Temple of Concord
cityEvents.summary: Cicero led Lentulus by the hand from the Palatine to the Temple of Concord, where the senate heard the envoys and opened the sealed letters; Lentulus was made to resign his praetorship.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Concord

cityEvents.title: Caesar and Cato debate the conspirators' fate
cityEvents.summary: In the Temple of Concord, ringed by armed knights, Caesar argued for life imprisonment in Italian towns; Cato's speech for death carried the house.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Concord

cityEvents.title: The Catilinarians strangled in the Tullianum: 'Vixerunt'
cityEvents.summary: Cicero led Lentulus down from the Palatine through the Forum to the Carcer, and the executioners strangled him, Cethegus, Statilius, Gabinius and Caeparius in the Tullianum, a cell twelve feet underground. Cicero announced to the crowd: 'They have lived.'
cityEvents.locName: the Tullianum, lower chamber of the Carcer
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

cityEvents.title: Cicero buys Crassus' house on the Palatine
cityEvents.summary: Cicero borrowed to buy for 3.5 million sesterces the house of M. Crassus on the Palatine, formerly the house of Livius Drusus, overlooking the Forum, and joked that he was now so deep in debt he would join a conspiracy if anyone would have him.
cityEvents.locName: Cicero's house on the N slope of the Palatine above the Forum

cityEvents.title: Clodius in women's dress at the Bona Dea rites
cityEvents.summary: During the women-only rites of the Good Goddess in Caesar's official house, P. Clodius slipped in disguised as a lute girl; recognised by his voice, he was chased out and the rites were profaned. Caesar divorced his wife: 'Caesar's wife must be above suspicion.'
cityEvents.locName: the Domus Publica on the Sacra Via

cityEvents.title: Pompey's third triumph
cityEvents.summary: On his 45th birthday Pompey triumphed over fourteen nations, with placards recording 900 cities taken and an image of himself in pearls; he spent two days in the procession and did not need to kill the captive kings.
cityEvents.locName: triumphal route via the Sacra Via to the Capitol

cityEvents.title: Consul Bibulus drenched with dung on the Temple of Castor
cityEvents.summary: When Bibulus tried to block Caesar's agrarian law from the steps of the Temple of Castor, a basket of dung was emptied over his head, his fasces were smashed and two tribunes wounded. He shut himself in his house for the rest of the year.
cityEvents.locName: steps and speakers' platform of the Temple of Castor

cityEvents.title: Clodius turns the Temple of Castor into a fortress
cityEvents.summary: Clodius' gangs used the Temple of Castor as their stronghold in the Forum, storing arms there and tearing away its steps so it could not be stormed.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Castor, its steps removed

cityEvents.title: Clodius demolishes Cicero's house and builds a shrine of Liberty
cityEvents.summary: The day Cicero left for exile his Palatine house was plundered and burned; Clodius had the site consecrated to Libertas with a statue of a Greek courtesan from Tanagra and annexed part of it to his own neighbouring property.
cityEvents.locName: Cicero's house on the Palatine

cityEvents.title: Catullus' 'lewd tavern' at the ninth pillar from Castor
cityEvents.summary: Catullus attacks the regulars of 'the lusty tavern, the ninth pillar from the felt-capped brothers', the Temple of Castor and Pollux, where his girl now sits among them.
cityEvents.locName: a tavern under the colonnade nine pillars from the Temple of Castor (toward the Vicus Tuscus)
cityEvents.note: 'a pileatis nona fratribus pila'; the pillars were probably those of the porticoes along the Vicus Tuscus or the Basilica Sempronia.

cityEvents.title: Massacre in the Forum: Quintus Cicero left for dead
cityEvents.summary: When the bill to recall Cicero came before the assembly, Clodius' gladiators seized the Forum before dawn; the Tiber and the sewers were full of bodies and Quintus Cicero survived only by hiding under the corpses.
cityEvents.locName: the Forum and Comitium

cityEvents.title: Cicero welcomed back at the Porta Capena
cityEvents.summary: Returning from exile, Cicero found the steps of the temples at the Porta Capena crowded with the plebs; he walked through applauding crowds through the Forum to the Capitol.
cityEvents.locName: the Porta Capena and the temple steps around it

cityEvents.title: Clodius' gangs drive off the builders of Cicero's house
cityEvents.summary: On 3 November armed men drove the workmen off the site of Cicero's house, threw stones at the house of Quintus nearby and set it on fire; a week later Cicero himself was attacked on the Sacra Via and took refuge in a doorway.
cityEvents.locName: the building site of Cicero's house on the Palatine, and the Sacra Via

cityEvents.title: Clodius' slaves storm the Megalesian games
cityEvents.summary: During the plays of the Megalesia, held before the Temple of the Great Mother on the Palatine, the aedile Clodius let a mob of slaves burst into the audience, which Cicero denounced as a sacrilege.
cityEvents.locName: the theatre space before the Temple of Magna Mater, Palatine

cityEvents.title: The weeping elephants of Pompey's games
cityEvents.summary: Twenty elephants were matched against Gaetulian hunters in the Circus Maximus; wounded and terrified, they tried to break through the iron railings and trumpeted so piteously that the crowd rose in tears and cursed Pompey.
cityEvents.locName: arena of the Circus Maximus

cityEvents.title: Catullus searches all Rome for Camerius
cityEvents.summary: Looking for his friend, Catullus tries the Campus Minor, the Circus, all the bookshops, the temple of great Jupiter and Pompey's new portico, where he accosts the girls.
cityEvents.locName: the Porticus of Pompey (and the Campus, Circus, bookshops, Capitol)

cityEvents.title: Pompey dedicates his stone theatre
cityEvents.summary: Pompey opened Rome's first permanent theatre, crowned by a temple of Venus Victrix so that the seats could pass as the temple's steps, with lavish games including plays, athletes and five days of beast hunts.
cityEvents.locName: Theatre of Pompey and the Temple of Venus Victrix on top of its cavea

cityEvents.title: Great flood of the Tiber
cityEvents.summary: The Tiber flooded the low city, soaking the brick-built houses, many of which collapsed; Dio says it was taken as a sign from the gods over the restoration of Ptolemy.
cityEvents.locName: the low-lying Campus Martius and riverside

cityEvents.title: Caesar buys up land for a new forum
cityEvents.summary: Through Cicero and Oppius, Caesar paid 60 million sesterces for private houses NW of the Forum to clear the site of the Forum Iulium; at the same time Aemilius Paullus rebuilt the Basilica Aemilia.
cityEvents.locName: site of the Forum Iulium behind the Curia

cityEvents.title: The people bury Julia in the Campus Martius
cityEvents.summary: When Pompey's wife and Caesar's daughter died in childbirth, the crowd seized her body from the funeral at the Alban villa and buried it in the Campus Martius, a rare honour, against the consul's objection.
cityEvents.locName: tomb of Julia in the Campus Martius

cityEvents.title: Clodius' body burned in the Curia; the senate house burns down
cityEvents.summary: The day after Clodius was killed at Bovillae, his body was taken from his house on the Palatine to the Rostra; led by Sex. Cloelius the crowd carried it into the Curia Hostilia, built a pyre from benches, tables and the clerks' records, and burned it. The Curia and the adjoining Basilica Porcia were destroyed.
cityEvents.locName: inside the Curia Hostilia on the Comitium

cityEvents.title: Trial of Milo under Pompey's soldiers
cityEvents.summary: Milo was tried in the Forum ringed by Pompey's troops, while Pompey sat watching from the treasury by the Temple of Saturn. Unnerved by the soldiers and the Clodian crowd, Cicero spoke badly and Milo was condemned; the polished Pro Milone was written later.
cityEvents.locName: the Forum, with Pompey seated at the aerarium in the Temple of Saturn

cityEvents.title: Consul takes an axe to the doors of an Isis shrine
cityEvents.summary: When the senate ordered the shrines of Isis and Serapis demolished and no workman dared touch them, the consul L. Aemilius Paullus took off his toga, seized an axe and struck the doors himself.
cityEvents.locName: an Isis shrine (probably on the Capitol)
cityEvents.note: Valerius does not locate the shrine; Isis altars on the Capitol are attested in the 50s BC (Varro in Tertullian, Ad nat. 1.10).

cityEvents.title: Caesar breaks into the treasury in the Temple of Saturn
cityEvents.summary: When the tribune L. Metellus blocked the doors of the aerarium, Caesar told him it was harder for him to say than to do, and that he would kill him; the doors were forced and Caesar took the reserve, including the gold set aside against a Gallic invasion.
cityEvents.locName: the aerarium in the Temple of Saturn

cityEvents.title: Antony's troops storm the Forum against Dolabella
cityEvents.summary: The tribune Dolabella barricaded the Forum to force through debt cancellation; Antony sent soldiers down from the Capitol, smashed the tablets of the law and some 800 people were killed, some thrown from the Tarpeian rock.
cityEvents.locName: the Forum, entered from the Capitol

cityEvents.title: Caesar's naval battle in a basin in the Codeta
cityEvents.summary: For his triumphal games Caesar had a lake dug in the lesser Codeta for a sea battle between Tyrian and Egyptian fleets with thousands of rowers; it was filled in after a plague in 43.
cityEvents.locName: basin in the Codeta Minor, NW Campus Martius
cityEvents.note: The Codeta lay by the Tiber; whether the minor Codeta was in the Campus Martius or across the river is disputed.

cityEvents.title: Cleopatra lodged in Caesar's gardens across the Tiber
cityEvents.summary: Cleopatra stayed in Caesar's villa and gardens on the right bank of the Tiber, where Cicero visited and resented her arrogance; she left after the Ides of 44.
cityEvents.locName: Horti Caesaris on the right bank by the Via Portuensis

cityEvents.title: Crowds crushed at Caesar's triumphal games
cityEvents.summary: During Caesar's naval battle in the Codeta, crowds from all over Italy camped in tents in the streets and along the roads, and many people, including two senators, were crushed to death in the press.
cityEvents.locName: streets around the Campus Martius

cityEvents.title: Caesar's triumphal chariot breaks its axle in the Velabrum
cityEvents.summary: On the first day of his Gallic triumph, Caesar was nearly thrown out of his chariot when the axle broke in the Velabrum before the temple of Felicitas; he later climbed the steps of the Capitol on his knees, with forty elephants carrying torches on either side.
cityEvents.locName: the Velabrum, in front of the temple of Felicitas
cityEvents.note: Dio names the temple of Tyche (Felicitas) built by Lucullus; the triumphal route passed through the Velabrum toward the Forum.

cityEvents.title: Vercingetorix executed after the Gallic triumph
cityEvents.summary: Held for six years since Alesia, the Gallic leader walked in Caesar's triumph and was then put to death, by tradition in the Carcer.
cityEvents.locName: the Carcer Tullianum

cityEvents.title: Forum of Caesar and Temple of Venus Genetrix dedicated
cityEvents.summary: On the last day of his triumphs Caesar dedicated the Forum Iulium and the temple of his ancestress Venus Genetrix, with a gilded statue of Cleopatra beside the goddess, still unfinished.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Venus Genetrix at the head of the Forum Iulium

cityEvents.title: October Horse: Caesar's soldiers sacrificed on the Campus
cityEvents.summary: At the October festival the right-hand horse of the winning chariot was killed by the altar of Mars in the Campus Martius and the men of the Sacra Via and the Subura fought for its head, to nail it to the Regia or the Turris Mamilia. In 46 two rioting soldiers of Caesar were sacrificed in the same way and their heads hung on the Regia.
cityEvents.locName: the altar of Mars in the Campus Martius; heads to the Regia or the Turris Mamilia

cityEvents.title: Caesar's statue placed in the Temple of Quirinus
cityEvents.summary: The senate voted a statue of Caesar inscribed 'to the unconquered god' in the Temple of Quirinus, the deified Romulus, prompting Cicero's quip that he preferred Caesar to share a temple with Quirinus rather than with Salus.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Quirinus on the Quirinal

cityEvents.title: Antony offers Caesar the diadem at the Lupercalia
cityEvents.summary: Caesar sat on a golden chair on the Rostra watching the Lupercalia; Antony, naked but for the goatskin of a Lupercus, ran up and offered him a diadem wreathed with laurel. Caesar refused it to cheers and had it sent to Jupiter on the Capitol.
cityEvents.locName: the new Rostra at the NW end of the Forum

cityEvents.title: Calpurnia's dream; the doors of the house fly open
cityEvents.summary: On the night before the Ides the doors and windows of Caesar's bedroom burst open; Calpurnia dreamed the gable ornament of the house fell and she held her murdered husband in her arms, and begged him not to go to the senate.
cityEvents.locName: the Domus Publica on the Sacra Via

cityEvents.title: Caesar murdered at the foot of Pompey's statue
cityEvents.summary: At a meeting of the senate in the Curia of Pompey at the east end of Pompey's portico, the conspirators surrounded Caesar at his chair; stabbed 23 times, he covered his face with his toga and fell at the base of Pompey's statue, which ran with his blood.
cityEvents.locName: at the foot of Pompey's statue in the Curia of Pompey, behind Temples B and C at Largo Argentina
scholarship: Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)
cityEvents.note: The concrete foundation at the W edge of the Largo Argentina is identified as the Curia; Augustus later walled it up as a place of ill omen.

cityEvents.title: The assassins occupy the Capitol
cityEvents.summary: With the senate fled and the people silent, Brutus and the conspirators, with gladiators of Decimus Brutus, marched to the Capitol proclaiming liberty and barricaded themselves there.
cityEvents.locName: the Capitol

cityEvents.title: Three slaves carry Caesar's body home
cityEvents.summary: Caesar lay where he fell until three slaves put him on a litter and carried him home to the Domus Publica, one arm hanging down.
cityEvents.locName: from the Curia Pompeia to the Domus Publica on the Sacra Via

cityEvents.title: 'The Ides of March have come.' 'Yes, but not gone.'
cityEvents.summary: At the entrance to the meeting, after unfavourable sacrifices, Caesar mocked the haruspex Spurinna, who had warned him of danger until the Ides; Spurinna replied that the Ides had come but not gone.
cityEvents.locName: the entrance of the Curia of Pompey

cityEvents.title: Amnesty decreed in the Temple of Tellus
cityEvents.summary: Two days after the murder Antony convened the senate in the Temple of Tellus near his house in the Carinae; on Cicero's motion an amnesty was voted while Caesar's acts were confirmed.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Tellus, Carinae

cityEvents.title: Antony's funeral speech from the Rostra
cityEvents.summary: Caesar's body lay on an ivory couch in a gilded shrine modelled on the Temple of Venus Genetrix in front of the Rostra. Antony read the decrees of honours and the oaths of the senators to protect him, then held up the bloodstained toga; the crowd erupted.
cityEvents.locName: in front of the Rostra in the Forum

cityEvents.title: Caesar's body burned in the Forum
cityEvents.summary: Instead of letting the body go to the pyre built in the Campus Martius, the crowd heaped benches, tribunals and shop tables on the spot in the Forum and burned it there; veterans threw in their arms, women their jewels. The Temple of Divus Julius later rose where the pyre stood.
cityEvents.locName: the pyre site at the E end of the Forum, marked by the round altar in front of the Temple of Divus Julius
scholarship: Claridge, Rome: An Oxford Archaeological Guide (2nd ed. 2010)

cityEvents.title: The poet Helvius Cinna lynched by mistake
cityEvents.summary: Leaving Caesar's funeral, the poet Helvius Cinna was mistaken for the conspirator L. Cornelius Cinna; the crowd tore him to pieces and carried his head around on a spear.
cityEvents.locName: the Forum after the funeral

cityEvents.title: Column 'To the Father of his Country' at the pyre
cityEvents.summary: Caesarians led by the false Marius (Amatius) raised a column of Numidian marble and an altar at the cremation site inscribed 'Parenti Patriae'; the consul Dolabella had it demolished and the leaders thrown from the Tarpeian rock or crucified.
cityEvents.locName: the cremation site in the Forum

cityEvents.title: Antony seizes the treasure in the Temple of Ops
cityEvents.summary: Antony took the 700 million sesterces Caesar had deposited in the Temple of Ops on the Capitol, using it to pay his debts and buy support.
cityEvents.locName: Temple of Ops on the Capitol

cityEvents.title: The comet of the Ludi Victoriae Caesaris
cityEvents.summary: During Octavian's games in honour of Caesar's victories a comet blazed for seven days; the people took it for Caesar's soul received among the gods, and Octavian set a star on the head of Caesar's statue in the Temple of Venus Genetrix.
cityEvents.locName: statue of Caesar in the Temple of Venus Genetrix

cityEvents.title: The triumvirs post their proscription lists
cityEvents.summary: Antony, Octavian and Lepidus posted lists of the proscribed in the Forum, beginning with seventeen names and growing to some 300 senators and 2000 knights; heads were brought to the Rostra for the reward.
cityEvents.locName: the Forum and the Rostra

cityEvents.title: Cicero's head and hands nailed to the Rostra
cityEvents.summary: Antony ordered the head and the right hand that had written the Philippics nailed to the Rostra from which Cicero had spoken; Fulvia is said to have pierced the tongue with a hairpin. The crowd wept at the sight.
cityEvents.locName: the Rostra in the Forum

cityEvents.title: Caesar declared a god; temple voted on the pyre site
cityEvents.summary: On 1 January 42 the triumvirs had the senate swear to uphold Caesar's acts and recognise him as Divus Iulius, with a temple to be built at the place in the Forum where he had been cremated.
cityEvents.locName: the cremation site in the E Forum

cityEvents.title: A spring of oil gushes in Trastevere
cityEvents.summary: At the Taberna Meritoria, a hostel for veteran soldiers across the Tiber, oil was said to have welled from the ground and flowed all day. Christian writers later read it as a sign of Christ's coming, and the site was claimed by Santa Maria in Trastevere.
cityEvents.locName: the Taberna Meritoria across the Tiber (tradition: Santa Maria in Trastevere)
cityEvents.note: Date varies in the sources between 41 and 38 BC; association with S. Maria in Trastevere is medieval tradition.

cityEvents.title: Lightning on Octavian's Palatine house: Apollo claims the spot
cityEvents.summary: Octavian bought the house of the orator Hortensius and neighbouring plots on the Palatine; when lightning struck part of the site the haruspices declared that the god wanted it, and Octavian vowed there the Temple of Apollo.
cityEvents.locName: the house of Augustus beside the Temple of Apollo, SW Palatine
